point: PED compares percentage changes in quantity demanded and in price
exemplar: Price up 10%, quantity demanded down 5%: PED is -0.5.

point: PED has no units, so it compares goods with very different prices
exemplar: A 1% response is a 1% response, whether the good costs 50p or £500.

point: A price rise cuts quantity demanded, so PED has a minus sign
exemplar: Cinema tickets up 20%, visits down 10%: PED = -0.5, a negative number.

point: Each percentage change is the change divided by the original value, times 100
Keep the minus sign, because price and quantity demanded move in opposite ways
exemplar: Quantity -15%, price +25%: PED = -15 / 25 = -0.6.

point: Ignoring the sign, elastic means above 1 and inelastic means below 1
exemplar: PED of -2.5 is elastic; PED of -0.4 is inelastic.

point: When demand is price inelastic, raising the price raises total revenue
exemplar: PED -0.4: price up 10%, quantity down 4%, so spending rises.

point: PES shows how quantity supplied responds to a change in price
exemplar: Strawberry prices rise 20% and farms supply 5% more: PES = 0.25.

point: Spare capacity lets firms raise output quickly, so supply is elastic
exemplar: A half-empty factory can add a shift next week; a full one cannot.

point: PES is the % change in quantity supplied divided by the % change in price
exemplar: Price +10%, quantity supplied +5%: PES = 5 / 10 = 0.5.

point: PES is positive, because firms supply more when the price rises
exemplar: Both changes go the same way, so the answer has no minus sign.

point: YED divides % change in quantity demanded by % change in income
exemplar: Incomes rise 5% and holidays abroad rise 10%: YED = 2.

point: Positive YED means a normal good; negative YED means an inferior good
exemplar: Incomes rise and bus journeys fall: YED is negative, so buses are inferior here.

point: The tax raises firms' costs, so supply shifts up by the tax per unit
exemplar: A 50p tax per coffee moves the supply curve up by 50p at every quantity.

point: A specific tax gives a parallel shift and an ad valorem tax a pivot
exemplar: A 20% tax adds 20p to a £1 item but £1 to a £5 item, so the gap widens.

point: The more price inelastic demand is, the more of the tax consumers bear
exemplar: Smokers keep buying after a cigarette tax, so most of it shows up in the price.

point: When demand is price elastic, producers bear the larger share of the tax
exemplar: Tax one brand of crisps and buyers switch, so the firm absorbs most of it.

point: A tax equal to marginal external cost moves output to the social optimum
exemplar: If each tonne of smoke does £30 of harm to others, a £30 tax per tonne makes the firm count that harm.

point: Valuing the external cost in money is hard, so the tax rate is a guess
exemplar: How much is a day of a child's asthma worth in pounds? The tax depends on the answer.

point: With price inelastic demand, the tax cuts output by a small amount
exemplar: Drivers keep buying petrol after a fuel tax rise, so emissions fall a little.
